title: Maternal Distress during Pregnancy and Offspring Childhood Overweight.
ehr_evidence: We perform a cohort study using prospective data from 37,764 women and child dyads from the Danish National Birth Cohort (1996–2002). Computerised telephone interviews at approximately gestational weeks 16 and 30 and when the child was 6 and 18 months old were used to obtain information about prenatal exposures, maternal health, use of medicine, lifestyle, and the health and development of the child.
summary: A prospective cohort study of 37,764 Danish mother-child dyads from the Danish National Birth Cohort examining whether combined maternal distress (anxiety, depression, stress) during pregnancy was associated with childhood overweight at age 7.
key_findings: No association between maternal distress during pregnancy and childhood overweight at 7 years (adjusted OR 1.06, 95% CI 0.96–1.18).
In sex-stratified analyses, a modest (non-significant) increased risk in boys (OR 1.15, 95% CI 0.99–1.33) but not in girls (OR 0.98, 95% CI 0.85–1.13).
Prevalence of overweight at 7 years was 9.9% (8.7% in boys, 11.5% in girls).
Children of mothers who worried during pregnancy had a slightly increased risk of overweight (OR 1.10, 95% CI 1.00–1.22).
Lack of social support seemed slightly protective against childhood overweight (OR 0.93, 95% CI 0.82–1.04).
captured_features: Maternal distress combined score (anxiety, depression, stress) from SCL-92 and GHQ-60 interview items
Maternal anxiety, depression, and stress individual scores
Child BMI and childhood overweight status (95th percentile Cole et al. reference)
population: 37,764 Danish mother-child dyads from the Danish National Birth Cohort (1996–2002); children aged ~7 years (age span 5–8, 80% aged 7), Denmark
exposure_domain: Psychosocial/psychological stress (maternal anxiety, depression, and stress during pregnancy)
limitations: Maternal distress exposure was self-reported via telephone interviews, risking misclassification.
Childhood overweight outcome was based on self-reported parental weight/height data, introducing measurement error.
Approximately 40% of initial participants were lost to the 7-year follow-up, raising selection bias concerns.
Low exposure contrast due to a relatively healthy, higher-socioeconomic-status population.
